449.title: Share your coat (Luke 3:1–20)
449.hook: John tells soldiers and tax collectors to be fair and share
449.howItsDone: Catholics hear John the Baptist's preaching in Advent, and some parishes run coat and clothing drives in winter; clothing the naked is one of the corporal works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the boy Jesus was lost and found in the Temple, and then he grew. Your line was growing is holy. A new week starts.

Luke opens chapter three like a historian dating a document. In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar. Pontius Pilate governor of Judea. Herod tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the next region over, Lysanias of Abilina. Annas and Caiphas the high priests. A roll call of power, lined up in order. And then: the word of the Lord came to John, the son of Zachary, in the desert. Not to any of them. To a man in the wilderness.
screen: `THE FIFTEENTH YEAR OF TIBERIUS.` → `A ROLL CALL OF POWER, IN ORDER.` → `THE WORD CAME TO JOHN, IN THE DESERT.`

segments.voice: John comes into the country around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of penance for the forgiveness of sins, as Isaias had written: a voice of one crying in the wilderness, prepare ye the way of the Lord. Crowds come out to be baptized, and he doesn't flatter them. Brood of vipers, he calls them. Don't tell yourselves you're safe because Abraham is your father. The axe is already laid to the root of the trees. Shaken, the crowds ask: then what shall we do? His answer is surprisingly ordinary. In the Douay-Rheims: "He that hath two coats, let him give to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do in like manner." The publicans, the tax collectors, ask: and us? Don't collect more than you're supposed to. Soldiers ask too: don't bully anyone, don't accuse anyone falsely, and be content with your pay. He doesn't tell the tax collectors to quit, or the soldiers to desert. He tells them to be honest and fair where they already are. The coat in his first answer is a chiton, the tunic worn under the outer cloak. If you have two, one is a spare. John's preaching points past himself, to one coming who is mightier, whose sandal strap he isn't worthy to untie. And Luke ends the scene with what that honesty cost him: Herod, rebuked by John, shut him up in prison.

segments.voice: Picture your closet, or the hooks by your door, and go through it slowly in your mind until you find something warm you have two of, or haven't worn in a year. Think of where it could go: a shelter, a parish clothing drive, someone you know who's cold. Then ask the crowd's question about the rest of your life, what shall I do, right where I am, and if you pray, offer the answer to God.

Your line: two coats, give one. Fair and honest, right where you are. See you tomorrow.

450.title: Son of Adam (Luke 3:23–38)
450.hook: Luke's family tree goes back to Adam, son of God
450.howItsDone: At every Mass the Universal Prayer, or prayers of the faithful, asks God's help for the Church, the world, and all people in need, the whole human family.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the chiton: John told everyone to be fair right where they were. Your line was two coats, give one.

Lists of names in the Bible are easy to skim. But look where Luke puts his. Jesus has just been baptized in the Jordan. The heavens open, the Holy Ghost comes down in bodily shape like a dove, and a voice from heaven says: thou art my beloved Son; in thee I am well pleased. And right there, before Jesus says a word in public, Luke stops the story for a family tree. Where he puts it matters, and where it ends matters more.
screen: `EASY TO SKIM.` → `THOU ART MY BELOVED SON.` → `THEN, A FAMILY TREE.`

segments.voice: It starts, in the Douay-Rheims: "And Jesus himself was beginning about the age of thirty years; being (as it was supposed) the son of Joseph." As it was supposed. Luke has already told us about the angel and Mary, and he doesn't let us forget it, even here. Then the list runs backward, father by father: Heli, Matthat, a long run of names, then David, Jesse, Judah, Isaac, Abraham. And it keeps going, past Abraham, past Noah, to the last line: "Who was of Henos, who was of Seth, who was of Adam, who was of God." Matthew's family tree runs forward and starts with Abraham, the father of Israel. Luke's runs backward, all the way to Adam. And adam, in Hebrew, is also the ordinary word for a human being; Genesis sets it beside adamah, the ground he was formed from. Christians read Luke's list as saying that this beloved Son belongs not only to one people, but to the whole human family. An honest note: between David and Joseph, Matthew and Luke give mostly different names, and the Gospels never explain why. Christian writers have proposed answers: that one list traces Joseph's line and the other Mary's, or, from an early writer named Julius Africanus, that a custom of marrying a brother's widow gave Joseph both a natural and a legal father. The Church hasn't settled on one. Either way, Luke's list ends where he wants you to look: son of Adam, son of God.

segments.voice: Start with the people closest to you and hold them for a breath; then widen to your street, your town, the people you passed today without noticing; then wider still, to strangers, people who speak languages you don't know, people you find hard to love. Luke's list runs back to one father, Adam, for all of them. If you pray, pray for them together, the whole human family; if not, let the circle stay that wide for a minute.

451.title: The Nazareth sermon (Luke 4:16–30)
451.hook: good news to the poor, sight to the blind, freedom to captives
451.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke 4:16–21 at the Chrism Mass of Holy Week, when the bishop blesses the holy oils, and on a Sunday in Ordinary Time in the year of Luke's Gospel.

segments.voice: Yesterday, adam: Luke's family tree ran back past Abraham to Adam, son of God. Your line was everyone's family.

After the desert, Jesus comes back to Galilee, and word about him spreads. Then he goes home to Nazareth, where he was brought up. On the Sabbath he goes into the synagogue, as was his custom. These people watched him grow up and know his family. He stands up to read, the attendant hands him the scroll of the prophet Isaias, and he unrolls it and finds the place he's looking for.
screen: `HOME TO NAZARETH.` → `AS WAS HIS CUSTOM.` → `THE SCROLL OF ISAIAS.`

segments.voice: He reads, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me. Wherefore he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor." And on: to heal the contrite of heart, to preach deliverance to the captives and sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, to preach the acceptable year of the Lord. Anointed is the root of the title Christ: Christos, the anointed one, in Hebrew Messiah. The acceptable year echoes the jubilee in the law of Moses, when land went back to its families and those sold into service went free. Then he rolls up the scroll and sits down, the posture of a teacher. Every eye is on him. And the sermon Luke gives us is one sentence: "This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears." At first they marvel at his gracious words. Then someone says: isn't this Joseph's son? Jesus answers that no prophet is accepted in his own country, and reminds them of two old stories we read a few weeks ago: Elias was sent not to the widows of Israel but to a widow in Sarepta of Sidon; Eliseus healed not the lepers of Israel but Naaman the Syrian. God's blessing, going to outsiders. The hometown crowd is filled with anger, and they drive him to the brow of the hill to throw him down. But he, passing through the midst of them, went his way. Luke puts this near the start of the ministry, and some readers hear it as a program for all that follows: good news for the poor, and a welcome wider than anyone expected.

Let each phrase land on a real person you know: someone poor, someone heartbroken, someone stuck. If you pray, hold each of them before God.

452.title: Depart from me (Luke 5:1–11)
452.hook: after the great catch Peter falls down: I am a sinful man
452.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's call of Peter at Sunday Mass in the year Luke's Gospel is read, and before Communion the whole congregation says aloud that they are not worthy, asking the Lord only to say the word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jesus read Isaiah in the Nazareth synagogue: Christos, the anointed one. Your line was good news to the poor.

Fishermen on the lake of Genesareth worked at night, when the fish came up toward the surface. So picture the morning. Simon and his partners have been out all night and caught nothing. They're on the shore, washing their nets, tired and done. A crowd presses in on a teacher, who climbs into Simon's boat and asks him to push off a little, so he can talk to the people from the water. When he's finished, he says what no tired fisherman wants to hear: go back out. Let down your nets again. In the daytime.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `A TEACHER IN SIMON'S BOAT.` → `PUT OUT INTO THE DEEP.`

segments.voice: Simon's answer is honest and a little weary: "Master, we have laboured all the night, and have taken nothing: but at thy word I will let down the net." And the nets fill so full they begin to break. He waves for the other boat, James and John, and both boats load up until they start to sink. You'd expect a fisherman to celebrate. Instead Luke says Simon Peter fell down at Jesus' knees: "Depart from me, for I am a sinful man, O Lord." It's strange. Nobody accused Peter of anything. But being that close to something holy made him see himself clearly, and what he saw made him want distance. Isaiah felt it in the Temple, crying out that he was a man of unclean lips. Jesus doesn't argue with Peter about whether he's a sinner. He doesn't leave, either. He says: "Fear not: from henceforth thou shalt catch men." Peter asks for distance and gets a job. Then a quiet line: they brought their boats to land, and leaving all things, they followed him. Catholics hear an echo of this at every Mass. Just before Communion, the people say they are not worthy to receive the Lord, and ask him only to say the word. Those words come from a Roman centurion a little later in Luke, but the instinct is Peter's on the beach: I'm not ready for you to come this close. And in both stories, he comes anyway.
screen: `AT THY WORD I WILL LET DOWN THE NET.` · `THE NETS BREAK, THE BOATS SINK.` · `PETER ASKS FOR DISTANCE.` · `FEAR NOT: YOU'LL CATCH PEOPLE.` · then, large: `DEPART FROM ME, FOR I AM A SINFUL MAN.`

segments.voice: Notice one thing in you that makes you want to keep God, or anyone good, at arm's length: a habit, a regret, a mood you're in today. Don't fix it; just name it, the way Peter named his, and then picture the answer he got: not a lecture, just fear not, and an invitation to stay in the boat. If you pray, say Peter's words, and rest in the silence after them.

453.title: Blessed are you poor (Luke 6:20–26)
453.hook: Luke's beatitudes are blunt, with woes to the rich
453.howItsDone: Catholics hear Luke's sermon on the plain at Sunday Mass in the year of Luke's Gospel, and parishes run food pantries, Saint Vincent de Paul conferences and collections for the poor as a regular part of parish life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, on the lake of Genesareth, a boat full of fish, and Peter asking Jesus to depart. Your line was fear not.

Matthew sets the beatitudes on a mountain: blessed are the poor in spirit. Luke tells a different scene. Jesus has spent the night praying on a mountain, picked his twelve, and come down. He stands, Luke says, in a plain place, a level stretch of ground, with a great crowd from Judea, Jerusalem and the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon. Sick people push to touch him. He lifts his eyes to his disciples and speaks, and what he says is shorter than Matthew's version, and sharper.
screen: `A NIGHT OF PRAYER, THEN DOWN.` → `A PLAIN PLACE, A GREAT CROWD.` → `SHORTER, AND SHARPER.`

segments.voice: Luke's first beatitude, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed are ye poor, for yours is the kingdom of God." Not poor in spirit. Poor. And not they. You. Jesus is looking at real people in front of him and talking straight to them. Luke has four blessings: you poor, you who hunger now, you who weep now, you who are hated for his sake. Then he turns the coin over with four woes. The first: "But woe to you that are rich: for you have your consolation." Woe to you that are filled, for you shall hunger. Woe to you that now laugh. Woe when all men speak well of you. Each blessing has its matching woe. Some readers hear woe not as a curse but as a cry of grief: alas for you. On that reading, Jesus isn't wishing harm on the comfortable; he's warning that comfort can be the whole reward, and then it's spent. So which is it, poor or poor in spirit? Catholics read both Gospels as true and hold them together. Matthew names the heart that knows it needs God. Luke won't let that become only an inner feeling: real hunger and real poverty are what God sees first. The Catechism speaks of the Church's preferential love for the poor, and says that love is inspired by the Gospel of the beatitudes. Some saints took Luke literally. Francis of Assisi handed even his clothes back to his father, in front of the bishop, and walked away with nothing.
screen: `NOT POOR IN SPIRIT. POOR.` · `FOUR BLESSINGS, FOUR WOES.` · `WOE AS A CRY: ALAS FOR YOU.` · `A PREFERENTIAL LOVE FOR THE POOR.` · then, large: `BLESSED ARE YE POOR.`

segments.voice: Think of who you're likely to pass today: someone outside a store, a coworker who's struggling, a family on a parish list. Pick one, decide what you could give, money, food, time, a real conversation, and picture looking them in the eye, the way Jesus looked at the crowd on the plain, as people he called blessed. If you pray, hold that person before God by name.

454.title: Love your enemies (Luke 6:27–38)
454.hook: good measure, pressed down, shaken together, running over
454.howItsDone: Catholics pray for enemies in personal prayer and in the prayers of the faithful at Mass; forgiving offenses and praying for the living and the dead are among the Church's spiritual works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sermon on the plain began with four blessings and four woes. Your line was blessed are you poor.

A grain seller dips a measuring basket. A stingy seller scoops loosely, so there's air in it. A generous one fills it, presses it down with his hands, gives it a shake so the grain settles, and fills it again until it heaps and spills over the rim. Then he pours it into the fold of your robe. You walk away with more than you paid for. Jesus ends a hard teaching with that picture.
screen: `A MEASURING BASKET AT A STALL.` → `PRESSED, SHAKEN, SPILLING OVER.` → `POURED INTO YOUR LAP.`

segments.voice: The sermon on the plain keeps going, and it gets harder. "But I say to you that hear: Love your enemies, do good to them that hate you." Then, one after another: bless those who curse you. Pray for those who mistreat you. If someone strikes you on one cheek, offer the other. Give to everyone who asks. Do to others as you'd have them do to you. Love here is not a feeling. Every item is an action: do good, bless, pray, give. Jesus doesn't ask you to like your enemy. He asks you to act for their good. Then the reason: be merciful, as your Father also is merciful; God, he says, is kind to the ungrateful and the evil. And then the picture from the market: "Give, and it shall be given to you: good measure and pressed down and shaken together and running over shall they give into your bosom." With the same measure you use, it will be measured back to you. That's not a business deal. It's about the size of the basket you carry. Luke also wrote the Acts of the Apostles, and he shows it happening: Stephen, dying under the stones, prays for the people throwing them. The command is hard, and Luke doesn't soften it. But it never says an enemy stops being dangerous. Loving an enemy can mean keeping a safe distance and still praying for them.
screen: `LOVE HERE IS ACTION, NOT FEELING.` · `BE MERCIFUL, AS YOUR FATHER IS.` · `THE SIZE OF YOUR BASKET.` · `STEPHEN PRAYS UNDER THE STONES.` · then, large: `GOOD MEASURE, RUNNING OVER.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind who has hurt you or works against you; it doesn't have to be the worst one, start small. Say their name inside once, and notice what happens in your chest. If you pray, ask God for one good thing for them, health, peace, a better day than they gave you; if you don't, simply wish it for them, because you don't have to feel warm to do it.

455.title: The widow of Naim (Luke 7:11–17)
455.hook: Jesus stops a funeral because he had compassion on the mother
455.howItsDone: Comforting the sorrowful is one of the Church's spiritual works of mercy, and some Catholic parishes send people to sit with grieving families, bring meals, and pray with them at the funeral vigil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, agape: love that acts, even for an enemy, with a measure running over. Your line was good measure. Today ends the week.

Two crowds meet at a town gate. One is coming out: a funeral, with a large crowd from the town walking beside the bier. On it lies a young man, the only son of his mother, and she is a widow. The other crowd is coming in, following Jesus and his disciples up the road. The town is Naim. Nobody asks Jesus for anything.
screen: `TWO CROWDS AT A TOWN GATE.` → `AN ONLY SON, A WIDOWED MOTHER.` → `NOBODY ASKS.`

segments.voice: Luke tells it in seven verses. The turning point: "And when the Lord had seen her, being moved with mercy towards her, he said to her: Weep not." Look at the order. He sees her first. Not the dead son, the mother. Luke has already told us what is at stake for her: she is a widow, and this was her only son. Then he's moved. Luke's Greek word for it comes from the word for the inner organs, the gut: the feeling that grabs you in the stomach. Then he speaks to her: weep not. Only then does he touch the bier, and the bearers stop. "Young man, I say to thee, arise." The young man sits up and begins to speak, and Luke adds the gentlest line in the story: he delivered him to his mother. Not to the crowd. To her. The people respond with fear and praise: a great prophet has risen among us, and God has visited his people. Readers hear an echo of Elias, who raised a widow's son at Sarephta long before, in the Third Book of Kings in the Douay. Luke is the only Gospel that tells this story, and he notices widows again and again: Anna in the Temple, the widow who keeps coming back to an unjust judge, the widow with two small coins. Catholics hear it as a picture of how God looks at grief. Before anything is fixed, someone sees you, is moved, and speaks to you. Weep not isn't a scolding. It's what you say to a person when you're about to help.
screen: `HE SEES THE MOTHER FIRST.` · `MOVED IN THE GUT.` · `YOUNG MAN, ARISE.` · `HE GAVE HIM TO HIS MOTHER.` · then, large: `WEEP NOT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you know who is grieving right now: a death, a divorce, a diagnosis, a child far away. Picture them the way Jesus saw the widow at the gate, let yourself feel it in the gut, and think of one small thing that might help: a message, a meal, sitting with them, saying the name of the one they lost. If you pray, hold them before God.
Naim. The town gate where a widow's only son lay on the bier, and Jesus saw her, moved with compassion, before anyone asked. Today's word.
Your line: weep not. That's week sixty-five, from two coats to the gate of Naim. Day four hundred fifty-five, done.
